planting.note: Plant in early spring after frost danger passes; like standard boysenberry, this trailing type needs a stout two- or three-wire trellis, but the thornless canes are far easier to train and harvest by hand.

directions: Thornless Boysenberry is a spineless sport of the classic boysenberry, carrying the same rich, deep maroon-purple, winey-flavored fruit but on canes free of the vicious thorns that make standard boysenberry a challenge to prune and pick. Yield and berry size run slightly behind the thorny original in most trials, and the thornless canes can be a touch less vigorous, but the dramatically easier hand harvest and maintenance make it the preferred choice for home gardens. Train canes to a trellis at 3 and 5 feet, cut all fruited canes to the ground right after summer harvest, and tie in the new season's canes to the wires for the following year's crop. In the cooler end of its range, canes can be unclipped from the wires and laid on the ground under mulch for winter protection.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide

planting.note: Plant rooted tip cuttings or bare-root canes in early spring and install a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft at the same time. Buckingham is thornless, unlike the original tayberry, which makes trellising and harvest considerably easier.

directions: Buckingham is a thornless Scottish-bred tayberry selection, carrying the same long, conical, deep purple-red berries and rich, sweet-tart raspberry-blackberry flavor as the original tayberry but on spineless canes that are much more pleasant to train, prune, and hand-pick. Fan-train the long trailing canes along wires, keeping the current season's primocanes separated from the fruiting floricanes to simplify post-harvest cleanup. Cut fruited canes to the ground immediately after harvest and tie the new canes onto the wires for next year's crop. In the cooler part of its range, detach canes from the trellis after leaf drop and cover with straw mulch or row cover for winter protection; in the humid Gulf South, prioritize good air circulation and a well-drained, elevated bed to reduce cane and fruit rot pressure.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — RHS Fruit Garden Displayed
Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide
University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring and install a sturdy trellis at planting time; Columbia Star is a vigorous thornless trailing blackberry that needs generous wire spacing to accommodate its long canes.

directions: Columbia Star is a USDA-Oregon State University thornless trailing blackberry bred for very large, firm, glossy-black berries with excellent, well-balanced sweet flavor, developed as a fresh-market improvement over older Pacific Northwest trailing cultivars like Marion. Canes are extremely vigorous and need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and generous plant spacing to manage their length. Train fruiting canes along the wires and remove them at ground level right after harvest, tying in the current season's new primocanes to bear next year's crop. Trailing blackberries of this type are bred primarily for the cool, dry summers of the Pacific Northwest and can struggle with fungal disease pressure in humid climates, so in the Gulf South prioritize excellent air circulation, full sun, and well-drained raised beds.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Small Fruit Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring and install a sturdy trellis at planting time; Black Diamond is a vigorous thornless trailing blackberry that needs generous wire spacing to accommodate its long canes.

directions: Black Diamond is a Washington State University thornless trailing blackberry developed as a machine-harvestable processing cultivar, prized for large, firm, jet-black berries with a mild, sweet flavor and good post-harvest storage compared to older trailing types. Vigorous, long canes require a sturdy multi-wire trellis; fan-train fruiting canes along the wires and cut them to the ground immediately after harvest, tying in the new season's primocanes to bear the following year's crop. Like other Pacific Northwest trailing blackberries, Black Diamond is bred for cool, dry summers and is more disease-prone in hot, humid climates, so growers in the Gulf South should give it full sun, excellent air drainage, and a well-drained raised bed to reduce fungal pressure.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Small Fruit Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring and install a sturdy trellis at planting time; Silvan is a thorny, vigorous trailing blackberry, so wear heavy gloves when training and pruning.

directions: Silvan is an Australian-bred trailing blackberry (from the Victoria, Australia breeding program) known for very early ripening, large, glossy, dark-red-to-black berries, and rich, intense flavor closer to a wild blackberry than many milder modern cultivars. Unlike several newer trailing types, Silvan retains thorny canes, so heavy gloves are essential when fan-training the vigorous canes along a sturdy multi-wire trellis. Cut fruited canes to the ground right after harvest and tie in the current season's new primocanes for next year's crop. Silvan performs best in regions with cool, relatively dry summers; in humid climates give it full sun and excellent air circulation to limit fungal disease pressure on the ripening fruit.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide
